title: Boolean Data Types
learning_outcomes: Describe the purpose and main terms of Boolean Data Types.
Use or interpret an appropriate PostgreSQL example connected to true and false values.
Identify one edge case and select a safe way to verify the expected result.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on Boolean Data Types. Its primary job is to help you choose a type that accurately represents the value and its comparison, precision and storage needs. The listed PDF subtopics define the coverage expected here; work through them in order and connect each one to an example, edge case and checkable result.
content.why_it_matters: This topic matters because PostgreSQL systems must preserve correct results as data grows and more sessions or services interact with it. Practicing boolean data types teaches you to make assumptions explicit, apply the right SQL or operational tool, and verify behavior instead of relying on a demonstration that only worked once.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Keep the problem small: choose a type that accurately represents the value and its comparison, precision and storage needs. A PostgreSQL feature should be chosen for the semantics it provides, not just because it is available. Before executing a change, state the inputs, expected output and boundary conditions. The example below is intentionally small enough to inspect; it illustrates the idea but is not a substitute for a test against your schema and PostgreSQL version.

items.title: NULL in Boolean expressions
items.text: Treat NULL as unknown or absent: use IS NULL/IS NOT NULL and review how expressions and aggregates handle it.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Boolean Data Types
content_blocks.code: SELECT TRUE AND NOT FALSE AS allowed, (NULL::boolean IS UNKNOWN) AS unknown_state;
content_blocks.expected_output: Both columns return true; Boolean UNKNOWN is represented by NULL in SQL expressions.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For a read-only SELECT or inspection command, no reset is needed. For DDL/DML, use a disposable database; capture the starting state, run the example, inspect the result, and ROLLBACK or drop the lab objects as appropriate. Do not use production data or credentials.

content_blocks.title: Practical checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Version note: PostgreSQL 18.6 is the primary reference. PostgreSQL 19 beta/development features are not assumed to be stable.

task: Create a short practice artifact for “Boolean Data Types”: explain its goal, show one example linked to “True and false values”, state the expected result, and include one edge/failure case and verification method. Use a disposable database or static artifact as appropriate.
hints: Start with the listed subtopics, especially “True and false values”, and describe the expected behavior in your own words.
Run or inspect the smallest example that demonstrates the behavior; do not add unrelated features before it is verified.
When the result surprises you, capture the exact SQL/error, check version and permissions, and change one assumption at a time.
expected_output: A reviewable note or query for Boolean Data Types, with an explanation of “True and false values”, expected behavior, and a documented edge-case check.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying the example without checking its assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Object names, data types, privileges, extensions and data distribution affect database behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: List schema/version assumptions and test with a tiny synthetic dataset first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a single successful query as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: A happy-path result does not test invalid input, concurrent sessions, permissions, recovery or query performance.
common_mistakes.fix: Add one negative/edge case and record the evidence that confirms the expected behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Making a production change directly from a lesson.
common_mistakes.why: DDL, data updates, role changes and operational commands can affect data or availability.
common_mistakes.fix: Use an isolated lab, reviewed migration, least privilege, rollback/recovery plan and a second-person review for production.

summary: Boolean Data Types fits into the broader goal to choose a type that accurately represents the value and its comparison, precision and storage needs.
Use the curriculum subtopics as a completeness checklist: True and false values, Boolean expressions, Boolean columns.
State the schema/version assumptions and verify one normal case plus an edge case before trusting the result.
